Le maré tèt, tissu d’héritage et d’affir: The maré tèt, a fabric of heritage and affirmation

En recherchant des organismes venant en: While searching for organizations that help immigrant women facing domestic violence, I came across Femmes du monde in Côte-des-Neiges. As I browsed their schedule of activities, I stopped at a workshop devoted to the maré tèt, and my curiosity was immediately piqued… That’s how this article came to be.
<strong>À Montréal, dans un centre commu: In a Montréal community centre, fabrics pass from hand to hand, wrap around heads and become crowns. The maré tèt, born of a colonial law imposed on Black women in Louisiana, has become a symbol of Caribbean heritage, of passing things down and of sisterhood, carried by the laughter of the women gathered together.
Au cinquième étage d’un immeuble discret: On the fifth floor of an unassuming building in Côte-des-Neiges, an unusual workshop comes to life. From the street, nothing gives it away: on the ground floor, there is a community library and quiet hallways, but as you step out of the elevator, the atmosphere changes.
En entrant dans les locaux de Femmes du: Walking into the offices of Femmes du monde in Côte-des-Neiges, you are immediately struck by the warmth of the welcome. Children nestle in their mothers’ arms while conversations intertwine, as varied as the languages that carry them. Some are lively, others whispered, sometimes laden with painful confidences. Here, week after week, a network of mutual aid and solidarity is woven among women who have arrived with their stories, their struggles and their scars.
En ce premier jeudi d’août, une quinzain: On this first Thursday of August, about fifteen women gather around Christchna Pierre, one of the centre’s coordinators. In a glass-walled room at the back, flooded with light, the workshop tells the story of the maré tèt, as it is called in Antillean Creole. First, the community worker traces the history of the headwrap, from the plantations of the Americas to today’s streets, blending painful memory with cultural reclamation. Then it’s time for practice, where every gesture draws laughter and conversation, turning the workshop into a true moment of sharing and closeness.
<strong>De la Louisiane esclavagiste aux: From slaveholding Louisiana to the streets of Côte-des-Neiges
En 1786, en Louisiane coloniale, la soci: In 1786, in colonial Louisiana, society is governed by strict racial codes. These rules apply to a population in flux: enslaved people, migrants and gens de couleur, the name given to free Black people, whether born free or freed. Among these measures, one law stands out, revealing the social tensions of the late 18th century: the Tignon Law, or Chignon Law, which requires free Black women to cover their hair with a headscarf.
À cette époque, La Nouvelle-Orléans est: At the time, New Orleans is governed by Don Esteban Miró, representative of the Spanish crown. According to Caroline M. Dillman in her book Southern Women, interracial relationships — often forced and non-consensual, and already prohibited — heightened social tensions, particularly with white women. The birth of mixed-race children made this mixing, which the colonial codes sought to contain, even more visible. The number of free Black women was growing, along with their desire to integrate: they wore refined dresses, precious fabrics and dazzling jewellery.
Face à ce contexte, le gouverneur ordonn: Faced with this situation, the governor ordered free women of colour to cover their hair and give up any display of finery. The decree had two aims: to limit what the authorities perceived as an “attraction” encouraging interracial relationships, and to remind Black women, visibly, of the position of social inferiority assigned to them, even when free. In response, these women reinvented their hairstyles. They played with height, colours and styles, sometimes adding jewellery to elevate their creations. This gesture became an act of resistance and creativity that endures to this day.
Les lois encadrant l’esclavage et le sta: The laws governing slavery and the status of free people varied depending on the colonial power. Spain relied on Las Siete Partidas, an ancient legal compilation poorly suited to the realities of the Americas. After 1685, the French colonies applied the Code noir, designed to regulate the lives of enslaved and freed people. As for the English colonies, they adopted their own local codes.
Plus de deux siècles plus tard, le foula: More than two centuries later, the headwrap has lost none of its symbolic force. For Christchna, a community worker who wears the maré tèt every day, it is far more than an accessory. “I started wearing it when I was young. It’s a gesture that gives me confidence and empowerment,” she says.
Pour elle, chaque foulard raconte une hi: For her, every headwrap tells a story. “You can see a Black woman walking down the street in a maré tèt and think it’s just fashion. But behind it there’s a history of repression and, today, of reclamation,” the community worker explains. Her attachment to the headwrap is as personal as it is cultural. It is an art she learned as a teenager and perfected by drawing inspiration from role models like Paola Maté, a Haitian entrepreneur she admires.
Au fil de l’après-midi, l’énergie collec: As the afternoon goes on, the collective energy in the room is palpable. The participants settle in, open their bags, take out their headwraps and discuss the colours, the textures and the stories each fabric carries. Impatience sets in: everyone is eager to tie her own.
Le cours se tient en français et en angl: The class is held in French and English, and very quickly, something magical happens: despite the different languages, the participants understand each other without a word, through gestures, glances and bursts of laughter.
« Encore une fois, l’homme veut dominer: “Once again, man wants to dominate woman,” calls out a participant at the back of the room. Laughter erupts. Another quickly replies: “They wanted to make them less beautiful, but now they’re all we see… these women are even more magnificent.” A dialogue takes hold, and each woman adds her own colour, her own perspective. It is no longer just a class, but a real exchange.
Les tissus circulent de main en main, em: The fabrics pass from hand to hand, carrying laughter, anecdotes and advice along with them. Christchna demonstrates three different ways to tie the headwrap. Each demonstration sparks applause, smiles and compliments, turning the workshop into a lively mini fashion show. Soon, the whole room is transformed into a living tableau: every head wears a small crown, celebrating each woman’s history, identity and creativity alike.
L’organisme Femmes du monde de Côte-des-: The organization Femmes du monde de Côte-des-Neiges has managed to turn this cultural heritage into a true space for popular education. “In our workshops, the goal isn’t only to show how to tie the headwrap, but also to deconstruct systems of oppression and discuss each person’s reality,” explains the co-coordinator.
Certaines participantes découvrent, à tr: Some participants discover, through this headwrap, a history they never suspected. Jasmine, a participant originally from Saint Vincent, remembers wearing it every day to protect herself from the sun when she worked at the market. Charmed by the way Christchna tied her headwrap, she suggested creating the workshop. “I didn’t know the history behind the headwrap. Now it makes me want to wear it every day,” she says with a smile.
Pour Christchna, l’intention allait bien: For Christchna, the intention went well beyond a simple aesthetic exercise. “With this workshop, I wanted to show that fashion can be political and a way to survive,” she explains. She adds that she is not an expert on this piece of cloth, and that while women from many cultures wear it — often in different ways, as in West Africa — the workshop focuses on the history of the Americas.
Pour Natina, Italienne installée au Québ: For Natina, an Italian who has long lived in Quebec, the headwrap awakened a childhood memory: “When I was 10, they dressed me in a traditional costume and put a scarf on my head.” She smiles as she recalls the episode, then adds: “At first, I was hesitant to take part because it’s not my culture. But the community worker was so inclusive that I thought, ‘Why not?’”
Celui qu’elle a porté lors de l’atelier: The one she wore during the workshop is very different, but the experience brought her back to that intimate memory. Like an invisible thread connecting cultures, the headwrap crosses eras and continents.
<strong>Un havre de sororité au cœur de: A haven of sisterhood in the heart of Côte-des-Neiges
Depuis plus de vingt ans, Femmes du mond: For more than twenty years, Femmes du monde has offered women of all backgrounds a place to meet, talk and support one another. On the walls, colourful photos and posters tell the story of the community kitchens, language workshops, movie nights and support groups.
Mais derrière cet agenda bien chargé, le: But behind this busy schedule, the realities are often harsh. “Many participants are living with both precarious immigration status and domestic violence. These situations intersect and complicate the support we provide,” the organization explains. Added to this are isolation and hidden homelessness, described gravely, in contrast with the centre’s vibrant energy.
Selon la co-coordonnatrice, Christchna P: According to co-coordinator Christchna Pierre, it is the intersectional and decolonial approach that sets the organization apart. “We support, we provide tools, but they are the ones who know what’s good for them,” she stresses. From discussions on homelessness to inclusive citizenship projects, every activity aims to break isolation and give power back to the participants.
